chapter: Harlem, 52nd Street and the first big bands
title: Harlem after-hours sessions at the Alexander Bar and Grill
summary: He describes the back room session at 126th and 7th where Chu Berry, Frank Newton and Ellington men jammed, police raids, and where he first heard Billie Holiday.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it

blocks.x: Oh, no. Not in public. There was plenty of it went on in sessions. I mean all the guys used to get together and not only in L.A., but in New York and Chicago and every other place. There'd always be a session going someplace. Particularly I remember up in -- this was a little later on, a couple of years later, but we always used to go up to the Alexander Bar and Grill, on the corner of 7th Avenue and 126th Street, up in Harlem, and they had a back room there. That's the first place I ever met Billie Holiday. She was --

At the end of Reel 1 you were just about to tell me about a place in -- or were you just starting to tell me -- in Harlem.

Oh, yes. The Alexander Bar and Grill on the corner of 126th Street and 7th Avenue. They had this room, this back room there, where there was a session every night. You'd go in there and there would be guys like Chu Berry and Johnny Russell and, oh, Frank Newton, and guys from the Ellington band, anybody that was around. And that's the first time I ran into Billie Holiday. She came in there and she was in bobby socks. The first time I ever heard her sing, they let her sing. It was quite a place, you know, before Prohibition was repealed. The cops would come in and raid the place and we'd go out on the street, and I guess the guy that owned the place had the fix in, and he would give us the sign, the minute the cops were gone, and we'd come right back in and start right in again.
Do you remember what guys from the Ellington band that you would run into in there?

Well, Barney Bigard was there, and let's see, Johnny Hodges I never saw there, but -- well, see, Rex was there, but he wasn't with Duke then. Rex I think was with Fletcher Henderson at the time. And there was a

trombone player there, his name escapes me, that played with Fletcher too. He used to be there. And I think Bill Coleman would drop in now and then. Oh, it actually depended who was in town. Any of the bands that came in town, they were -- oh, Louis Metcalf. Louis Metcalf used to come in there. He was at that time playing up with Vernon Andrade, at the Savoy Ballroom, and little Happy, the tenor man, was the -- he was the tenor man with Vernon Andrade. He was in there. I guess at one time or another most everybody was in there at some time. It wasn't a static group. It was subject to change.
Were there many white musicians who jammed in Harlem?

No. The group was, I would say, it might be -- I've been there when I was the only white guy, and I've been there when it was, you know, three or four more white guys there. There wasn't any -- you know, just whoever was there. And we all had a ball, we really did.
